Gregorian Mode. A system of eight melodic scales used in Gregorian chant and medieval liturgical music. Unlike the major and minor keys that dominate Western music since the Baroque period, each Gregorian mode has a distinct final, which is the ending note, analogous to a tonal center. Each mode has a characteristic range, creating different melodic characters and emotional associations. The modes were explicitly associated with liturgical function and emotional character, and their study remains foundational to understanding medieval and Renaissance music.

The eight Gregorian modes traditionally divide into four authentic modes with higher ranges and four plagal modes with lower ranges and more restricted tessitura, though the distinction is primarily pedagogical. The modes are numbered one through eight and named historically. The authentic modes are Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, and Mixolydian. The plagal counterparts are Hypodorian, Hypophrygian, Hypolydian, and Hypomixolydian.

Each mode has a distinctive melodic character. Dorian sounds minor-ish but brighter than modern minor. Lydian contains a raised fourth, like a major scale with a sharp four. Phrygian has a half-step above the final, creating an exotic, Spanish-sounding quality. The final is the melodic endpoint of a chant and the mode-determining anchor. It is not necessarily the lowest note, which varies by range. This distinguishes modes from modern scales where the root or tonic is typically lowest.

Each mode carried liturgical associations and emotional character. Dorian was solemn and authoritative. Lydian was bright and joyful. Phrygian was penitential. Mixolydian was festive and bold.

Gregorian modes are diatonic, built from the white keys of the piano in various configurations, using only natural notes without chromatic alterations. This was a fundamental constraint of medieval modal melody. The major and minor keys eventually replaced the modal system as harmonic, or vertical, thinking superseded purely melodic, or horizontal, organization. Yet modal thinking persists in jazz, folk music, and contemporary classical music. Gregorian modes remain the primary vehicle for understanding Gregorian chant in liturgical practice, and modal music represents the broader concept of mode-based melody and improvisation across cultures.
